name: Harbor rat
lede: Harbor rat is a muted greenish grey from Japan's traditional color list, one of a large family of "nezumi" (mouse-grey) names, and it is the rare traditional Japanese color whose top painter in our archive actually painted harbors.

sections.title: In Japan: Minatonezumi
sections.body:
The name is written 湊鼠, romanized Minatonezumi, and our color library glosses it literally as "harbor rat" [1]. *Nezumi* means mouse or rat, and it names a whole family of Edo-period greys, each one a mouse-grey tinted toward something else; who first paired this particular grey with a harbor is undocumented in the sources we have [1]. The closest named neighbors by measured color are [[colewort-green]] and [[concrete-grey]], both within about four units, with [[moss-grey]] and [[dusty-grey]] a little further out [2].

The hex value, #757D75, is a screen approximation; Japanese traditional names were fixed to dye and pigment, not to a monitor [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for Harbor rat in 643 of 23,781 paintings, about 2.7 percent, more common than 77 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 39 of 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.9 times the rate its share of the archive would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 34 percent of its appearances [3].

The painter most devoted to it is Eugène Boudin, in 5 of his 33 paintings here, 3.5 times his peers' rate, as photographed [3]. Boudin painted harbors and beaches most of his working life, which makes him an apt match for a grey named for one, though that is a coincidence of our archive and not evidence for the name's origin [3]. The earliest archive match is dated 1280, by Gao Kekong; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first [3]. It shares canvases more than chance with colors we call Traffic Grey B and Dawn Grey [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications [3].
